lead: QPSK carries two bits in each symbol by choosing one of four carrier phases. It is two BPSK signals on carriers 90° apart, so it sends twice the bits of BPSK in the same bandwidth with the same bit error probability. M-ary PSK goes further: with M = 2<sup>k</sup> phases each symbol carries k bits and the bandwidth per bit shrinks, but the points crowd together and need more power. QPSK runs satellite TV, LTE and Wi-Fi at their lower rates.
prereq: You need: BPSK and the idea of a two-dimensional signal space (see baseband data transmission and detection).

sections.h3: QPSK: two BPSK links on quadrature carriers

blocks.text: A is the amplitude in volts; I and Q are the two bits in bipolar form, each +1 or −1 (pure numbers); the symbol lasts T<sub>s</sub> = 2T<sub>b</sub>. The phase is arctan(Q/I) and the symbol energy is E<sub>s</sub> = A²T<sub>s</sub> = 2E<sub>b</sub> (1 Ω reference).

With the first bit of each pair setting I and the second setting Q (1 → +1, 0 → −1), the pairs land at 11 → 45°, 01 → 135°, 00 → 225° and 10 → 315°. Neighbours 90° apart differ in one bit only: this is Gray labelling.

items: Split the serial bits into two streams: odd-numbered bits to I, even-numbered bits to Q.
Make each stream bipolar NRZ and hold each level for T<sub>s</sub> = 2T<sub>b</sub>.
Multiply I by cos(2πf<sub>c</sub> t) and Q by −sin(2πf<sub>c</sub> t).
Add the two products and transmit.

blocks.text: Each branch runs at R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>/2 symbols per second, so with rectangular pulses the null-to-null bandwidth is 2R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>: half that of BPSK at the same bit rate. Some syllabi call QPSK 4-PSK or quadriphase shift keying.

The receiver multiplies r(t) by cos(2πf<sub>c</sub> t) and by −sin(2πf<sub>c</sub> t), integrates each over T<sub>s</sub> and takes the sign of each output: the I output gives the first bit and the Q output the second. Because the carriers are orthogonal over a symbol, each branch is a BPSK detector carrying one bit with energy E<sub>b</sub>.
Exactly the BPSK result. The symbol is right only if both bits are right, so P<sub>s</sub> = 1 − (1 − P<sub>b</sub>)² = 2P<sub>b</sub> − P<sub>b</sub>² ≈ 2P<sub>b</sub>.

A carrier phase error θ rotates the received constellation against the decision axes. The I output becomes A(I cos θ − Q sin θ)·Ts/2, so each decision picks up a part of the other bit (crosstalk) and the margin to the nearest boundary shrinks; at θ = 45° the points sit on the boundaries. Offset QPSK delays the Q stream by Tb so that the phase never jumps by 180°; it leads to MSK.

sections.h3: M-ary PSK: more phases, fewer hertz

blocks.text: M-ary PSK uses M equal-amplitude phases 2πm/M, m = 0, 1, …, M − 1, with M = 2<sup>k.</sup> Each symbol carries k = log<sub>2</sub> M bits (k = 1 is BPSK, k = 2 QPSK, k = 3 8-PSK). The symbol rate is R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>/k, the rectangular-pulse null-to-null bandwidth B = 2R<sub>s</sub> = 2R<sub>b</sub>/k and the bandwidth efficiency R<sub>b</sub>/B = k/2 b/s/Hz.

blocks.where: d is the distance between neighbouring points and E<sub>s</sub> = kE<sub>b</sub> the symbol energy. d = 1.414√E<sub>s</sub> for QPSK, 0.765√E<sub>s</sub> for 8-PSK, 0.390√E<sub>s</sub> for 16-PSK.

blocks.text: the symbol error probability for M ≥ 4 at high E<sub>s</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>. With Gray labels a symbol error usually changes one bit, so P<sub>b</sub> ≈ P<sub>s</sub>/k.

Going from k to k + 1 bits per symbol doubles M but multiplies the bandwidth per bit only by k/(k + 1): from QPSK to 8-PSK saves a third of the bandwidth, from 8-PSK to 16-PSK a quarter. Each step costs several dB, because d shrinks roughly in proportion to 1/M while E<sub>s</sub> grows only as log<sub>2</sub> M.

examples.question: A QPSK modem sends 10 Mb/s with rectangular pulses and Gray labels at E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 10 dB. Find (a) the symbol rate, (b) the null-to-null bandwidth, (c) the bandwidth efficiency, (d) P<sub>b</sub> and P<sub>s</sub>.
steps: k = 2, so R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>/2 = 5 Msymbol/s and T<sub>s</sub> = 0.2 µs.
examples.answer: R<sub>s</sub> = 5 Msymbol/s, B = 10 MHz, 1 b/s/Hz, P<sub>b</sub> = 3.87 × 10<sup>−6</sup>, P<sub>s</sub> = 7.74 × 10<sup>−6.</sup>

examples.question: The same 10 dB link is switched to 8-PSK with Gray labels. Find E<sub>s</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>, the neighbour distance in terms of √E<sub>s</sub>, P<sub>s</sub> and P<sub>b</sub>, and the bandwidth saved at 12 Mb/s compared with QPSK.
steps: Bandwidth at 12 Mb/s: QPSK 2 × 6 = 12 MHz; 8-PSK 2 × 4 = 8 MHz, a saving of one third.
Check: P<sub>b</sub> rose from 3.87 × 10<sup>−6</sup> to 1.01 × 10<sup>−3</sup>, about 260 times, for that third.
examples.answer: E<sub>s</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 30, d = 0.765√E<sub>s</sub>, P<sub>s</sub> ≈ 3.03 × 10<sup>−3</sup>, P<sub>b</sub> ≈ 1.01 × 10<sup>−3</sup>; 8 MHz instead of 12 MHz.

traps: R<sub>b</sub> and R<sub>s</sub> differ: a 10 Mb/s QPSK link runs at 5 Msymbol/s. Using 10 Msymbol/s doubles the bandwidth.
P<sub>b</sub> = Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)) uses E<sub>b</sub>. Putting E<sub>s</sub> = 2E<sub>b</sub> in its place makes QPSK look 3 dB better than it is.
In P<sub>s</sub> ≈ 2Q(√(2E<sub>s</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)·sin(π/M)) the angle is π/M, not π/k or 2π/M.
Gray labels lower P<sub>b</sub> for a given P<sub>s</sub>; they do not change P<sub>s</sub>, the points or the bandwidth.
Gray-label QPSK from the I and Q signs: (+,+) is 11 and (−,−) is 00. Swapping them breaks the bit mapping.

quiz.q: How many bits does a QPSK symbol carry, and how far apart in phase are neighbouring points?
Write the symbol rate and the bandwidth efficiency of M-ary PSK with rectangular pulses.
quiz.a: R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>/log<sub>2</sub> M; efficiency k/2 b/s/Hz with k = log<sub>2</sub> M.

quiz.q: Why does Gray-labelled QPSK have the same P<sub>b</sub> as BPSK at the same E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>?
quiz.a: Its I and Q branches are two independent BPSK detectors on orthogonal carriers, each carrying one bit with energy E<sub>b</sub>.

quiz.q: 8-PSK runs at 12 Mb/s with rectangular pulses. Find R<sub>s</sub>, B and the efficiency.
quiz.a: k = 3, R<sub>s</sub> = 4 Msymbol/s, B = 8 MHz, 1.5 b/s/Hz.

quiz.q: Find P<sub>b</sub> of QPSK at E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 8 dB.
Why does 16-PSK need much more power than QPSK for the same symbol error rate?
quiz.a: d = 0.390√E<sub>s</sub> against 1.414√E<sub>s</sub>. Keeping d needs (1.414/0.390)² = 13.1 times the symbol energy, 11.2 dB, and that energy now carries four bits instead of two.

quiz.q: A student says Gray labelling lowers the symbol error probability of QPSK. Correct it.
quiz.a: P<sub>s</sub> is unchanged; Gray labels only make most symbol errors cost one bit, so P<sub>b</sub> ≈ P<sub>s</sub>/2.

beyond: Not for the exam. π/4-QPSK rotates the constellation by 45° every symbol so the signal never passes through zero; APSK puts PSK points on several rings and is used by DVB-S2 satellite TV. A carrier loop can lock 90° off, so QPSK links add differential encoding or a known word to resolve the ambiguity. Search next: π/4-QPSK, APSK, phase ambiguity.

figure.caption: QPSK and 8-PSK on circles of the same symbol energy, with Gray labels: neighbours differ in one bit. The neighbour distance d falls from 1.414√E<sub>s</sub> to 0.765√E<sub>s</sub>, which is why 8-PSK needs more power for the same error rate.
